title: Indian American Former Optum Director Sentenced to Three Years in $950,000 Fraud Scheme
excerpt: Karan Gupta, 48, created a no-show job for a friend and pocketed kickbacks from his six-figure salary over three years, federal prosecutors said.
body:
• Karan Gupta, 48, of Walnut Creek, California, was sentenced to 36 months in federal prison on August 24 for defrauding Optum of more than $950,000.
  • Gupta hired his longtime friend Shangraf Kaul for a data engineering manager role despite Kaul lacking qualifications; Kaul performed no work for over three years while collecting a six-figure salary.
  • Gupta demanded approximately 60% of Kaul's salary as kickbacks, initially concealed through cash deposits and later through a shared checking account.
  • The scheme unraveled after Optum fired Gupta in November 2019 for a separate no-show employee fraud.

A federal judge in Minnesota has sentenced an Indian American former senior director at healthcare company Optum to three years in prison for orchestrating a fraud scheme that cost the UnitedHealth Group subsidiary more than $950,000.

Karan Gupta, 48, of Walnut Creek, California, received his sentence on August 24 from U.S. District Judge Kate M. Menendez. He had been convicted by a federal jury on February 17 following a six-day trial on one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, 10 counts of wire fraud, and one count of money laundering conspiracy.

The No-Show Job Arrangement

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Gupta hired his longtime friend Shangraf Kaul, 45, of East Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, as a data engineering manager on his team in late 2015. Prosecutors said Kaul lacked the qualifications for the position and performed no actual work at Optum for more than three years while receiving a six-figure salary that grew with raises and bonuses.

https://x.com/Simi28_/status/2092649729427386481

Gupta used his position as Kaul's supervisor to facilitate the arrangement and demanded that Kaul return approximately 60% of his unearned salary as kickbacks. The pair initially concealed the payments through cash deposits into Gupta's personal bank account. Kaul would withdraw the kickback amounts from his bank in New Jersey and deposit them at a New Jersey branch of Gupta's bank, which Gupta then accessed in California.

"Defrauding a private company is not a victimless crime. Gupta's actions ultimately undermine a healthcare provider that millions of Americans depend on, and today's sentencing reflects the seriousness of his crimes."

U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen

After several months, the two devised a more elaborate concealment method. Kaul opened a new checking account to receive his Optum direct deposits and sent the account's debit card to Gupta, who then withdrew the fraud proceeds through ATMs in California.

How the Scheme Unraveled

The fraud came to light after Optum terminated Gupta in November 2019 for his involvement in a separate no-show employee fraud scheme. The company launched an internal investigation and referred the matter to federal law enforcement. In total, Gupta's fraud against Optum exceeded $950,000, according to the Department of Justice.

FBI Minneapolis Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson said the case sends a clear message about corporate fraud accountability. "The FBI is committed to investigating complex fraud schemes that exploit trust and defraud victims through deliberate deception, including schemes in which the defendant creates a no-show position at the very company that employs him," Dotson said.

Co-Conspirator Awaits Sentencing

Kaul pleaded guilty on February 26, 2025, to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and is currently awaiting sentencing. Earlier reporting on the case noted that Gupta's total fraud against Optum may have exceeded $1.2 million when accounting for the full scope of Kaul's unearned compensation, including raises and bonuses over the multi-year period.

The case was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota, with investigation led by the FBI's Minneapolis field office. It adds to a series of high-profile fraud cases involving Indian American professionals in corporate and healthcare settings that have drawn federal attention in recent years.
